hook.question: A phone book has to stay sorted while new names are added and old ones are crossed out all day. How do you keep it quick to search without re-sorting the whole thing every time?
paragraphs: Keep the names in a sorted list and finding one is quick: open in the middle, drop half, repeat. But adding a name in the middle means sliding every name after it down one slot, and removing one means sliding them all back.

Keep the names in a chain of cards instead, and adding or removing is a link or two. But now finding a name means starting at the first card and flipping through them one by one. Is there a layout that is quick at both jobs?
hook.aha: Give every name a card with two arrows: one to the names that come before it, one to the names that come after. Finding a name becomes a game of "before or after?", and each answer drops everything on the other side. Adding or removing a name changes only a link or two. That is a binary search tree. It stays quick while it stays reasonably balanced, and a tree built from names that arrive already sorted does not.

metaphor: Think of a game of "higher or lower". At every node you hold one guess: if your number is lower you go through the left door, and if it is higher you go through the right door.
Each answer closes off a whole side of the tree, so you never look at most of it.
mentalModel.click: Every node asks "smaller or bigger?", and the answer rules out an entire subtree.

glossary.definition: For every node, all values in its left subtree are smaller and all values in its right subtree are bigger. It is about whole subtrees, not just the two children.
A node together with everything below it. Every node is the root of its own subtree.
Visit the left subtree, then the node, then the right subtree. On a BST this lists the values in sorted order.
The next bigger value after a node. When the node has a right subtree, it is the leftmost node in that subtree.
The number of links on the longest path from the root down to a leaf. Search, insert and delete take about this many steps.
Both sides of every node are about equally tall, so the height stays close to log n.
Leaning almost all one way, like a chain. Inserting values that are already sorted does this, and the height becomes n.

mentalModel.definition: A binary search tree is a binary tree in which, for every node, every value in its left subtree is smaller than the node's value and every value in its right subtree is larger. Reading it in order (left, node, right) lists the values sorted. Search, insert and delete each follow a single path from the root, so they take O(h) time, where h is the height of the tree: about log n when the tree is balanced, and up to n when it is skewed.

useWhen: You keep a collection of numbers sorted while values are added and removed, and you also look things up in it.
The problem hands you a TreeNode and says "binary search tree", or says the left side is smaller and the right side is bigger.
You need answers in order from a changing set: the next bigger value, the k-th smallest, everything in a range.
A sorted array would be perfect for lookups, but you would have to shift most of it on every insert or delete.
notWhen: The data never changes after you sort it: a sorted array with binary search is simpler and just as fast.
You only ask "is it in there?" and never need the order: a hash map answers in O(1) on average.
You only ever take the smallest or the largest item: a heap does that with less bookkeeping.

quiz.problem: Numbers arrive one at a time and some are removed. At any moment you must be able to say which stored value is the smallest one bigger than x.
options: heaps
hash-maps
bst
arrays
quiz.explanation: You need both updates and order. A BST keeps the values ordered, and the next bigger value is a short walk from the root. A heap only knows its minimum, a hash map has no order, and an array shifts on every insert.

quiz.problem: A pool of tasks keeps changing. All you ever need is to remove the task with the smallest deadline, again and again.
options: queues
bst
heaps
sorting
quiz.explanation: Only the extreme is ever needed. A heap does exactly that with less structure than a BST, which keeps the whole order that you would never use.

quiz.problem: A sorted array of 100,000 ids never changes. Answer, as fast as possible, whether a given id is in it.
options: binary-search
bst
hash-maps
linked-lists
quiz.explanation: Nothing is being inserted or deleted, so there is nothing for a tree to maintain. Halving the sorted array in place gets the same O(log n) with no extra pointers.

quiz.problem: Given the root of a binary tree, return its maximum depth, the number of nodes on the longest path from the root down to a leaf.
options: bst
trees
graphs
recursion
quiz.explanation: The values are never compared with each other, so no ordering is used. It is plain tree recursion: the depth is one more than the deeper of the two children.

quiz.problem: Given the root of a binary search tree and an integer k, return the k-th smallest value in the tree.
options: trees
heaps
sorting
bst
quiz.explanation: Reading a BST in order gives its values sorted, so the k-th smallest is the k-th node of an in-order walk. You don't need to build a heap or sort anything.

pseudocode.text: node = a new node holding val
hang node under parent, on the side val belongs

template.time: O(h): about O(log n) if balanced, O(n) in the worst case
notes: Search, insert and delete each walk one path from the root down, so they cost O(h), where h is the height.

h is about log n only while the tree stays balanced. Insert 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 in order and every value goes to the right of the last, so the tree is a chain and h is n. The Sorted input presets show it. Self-balancing trees (AVL, red-black) prevent this, and this lesson's plain BST does not.
Insert always ends in a new leaf and moves nothing else. This version sends a value equal to a node to the right; LeetCode's BST problems promise distinct values.

Delete has three cases: a leaf is cut off, a node with one child is replaced by that child, and a node with two children takes the value of its in-order successor, which is then removed as a leaf or a one-child node.
An in-order walk (left, node, right) of a BST visits the values in sorted order. That one fact solves k-th smallest, validate, and minimum difference.
To check a BST, compare each node with the whole range its ancestors allow, not just with its parent. Carry (lo, hi) down, and use null for "no bound yet" so INT_MIN and INT_MAX values still work.

examples.title: Search in a Binary Search Tree
examples.problem: Given the root of a binary search tree and an integer val, find the node whose value equals val and return the subtree rooted at that node. If there is no such node, return null.
approach: Start at the root, 4, and ask the BST question: is 2 equal to, smaller than, or bigger than this node? (The code calls the value key.)
2 < 4, so everything in the right subtree (7) is bigger than 4 and cannot hold 2. Go left to 2.
2 == 2, so return this node. Its subtree, 2 with children 1 and 3, prints as [2,1,3].
If curr ever becomes null, the value isn't in the tree, so return null. Each step drops a whole subtree, so the work is at most the height of the tree.

examples.title: Delete Node in a BST
examples.problem: Given the root of a binary search tree and a key, delete the node with that key, keeping the tree a valid binary search tree, and return the root of the updated tree.
approach: Search for 3 with parent trailing one step behind curr: from 5, go left to 3. Then count the children of 3.
3 has two children, 2 and 4, so you can't just cut it out. Take its in-order successor instead: go right once, then left as far as possible. The right subtree is just 4, so the successor is 4.
Copy 4 into the node that held 3, then remove the old 4. It is a leaf, so its parent's right link becomes null.
A leaf or a node with one child skips the copy: point the parent's link at the node's only child, or at null. The tree reads [5,4,6,2,null,null,7].

examples.title: Validate Binary Search Tree
examples.problem: Given the root of a binary tree, determine whether it is a valid binary search tree: every value in a node's left subtree is smaller than the node, and every value in its right subtree is larger.
approach: Comparing each node with only its children is not enough. In [5,4,6,null,null,3,7] every parent and child look right (4 < 5, 6 > 5, 3 < 6, 7 > 6), yet 3 sits in the right subtree of 5.
So carry an allowed range down: every node must be strictly between lo and hi. The root starts with no bounds.
Going left tightens hi to the node's value, and going right tightens lo. 3 is under 6, which is under 5, so its range is (5, 6), and 3 <= 5 fails.
Use "no bound yet" (None, null or nullptr) instead of a huge number as the starting bound, so nodes holding INT_MIN or INT_MAX still work.

conceptQuiz.question: Which statement is the BST invariant?
options: Each node's left child is smaller than it, and its right child is bigger.
Every value in a node's left subtree is smaller than the node, and every value in its right subtree is bigger.
The left subtree always has fewer nodes than the right subtree.
The tree is as short as it can possibly be.
conceptQuiz.explanation: The rule covers whole subtrees, not just the two children. Checking only children misses a value that sits on the wrong side of a node higher up.

conceptQuiz.question: You insert 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 in that order into an empty BST with no rebalancing. What does searching for 5 cost?
options: About 2 comparisons, because a BST balances itself.
1 comparison, because 5 is the biggest value.
5 comparisons: each value goes to the right of the last, so the tree is a chain and its height is n.
It can't be found: sorted input breaks a BST.
conceptQuiz.explanation: Every new value is bigger than everything so far, so it always goes right and the tree is a chain. O(log n) only holds while the tree is balanced; here the cost is O(n).

conceptQuiz.question: Why is the in-order successor a safe replacement when you delete a node with two children?
options: It is the smallest value on the right, so it is bigger than everything on the left and no bigger than anything else on the right.
It is always a leaf, so removing it changes nothing else.
It is the node closest to the root, so the tree gets shorter.
Any node from the right subtree would do. The successor is just the first one found.
conceptQuiz.explanation: Placing the smallest right-hand value in the gap keeps the left side smaller and the right side bigger. It may have a right child, which is lifted into its place, but it never has a left child.

conceptQuiz.question: What do you get by visiting a BST in order: left subtree, then the node, then the right subtree?
options: The values in the order they were inserted.
The values level by level, from the top down.
The values along a single path from the root.
The values in sorted order, smallest first.
conceptQuiz.explanation: Everything in the left subtree is smaller than the node and everything in the right subtree is bigger, so left, node, right comes out sorted. That is why in-order solves k-th smallest.

conceptQuiz.question: A tree has root 10 and left child 5, and 5's right child is 12. Every child is on the correct side of its own parent (5 < 10, and 12 > 5). Is it a valid BST?
options: Yes, every parent and child pair is in the right order.
No: 12 is in the left subtree of 10, so it would have to be smaller than 10.
Yes, as long as 5 has no left child.
No: a BST node may not have just one child.
conceptQuiz.explanation: The invariant is about whole subtrees. 12 is below 10 on the left side, so it must be less than 10, and it isn't. Checking only parent and child pairs would wrongly accept this tree.

practice.title: Insert into a Binary Search Tree
practice.insight: Walk down like a search. The first empty spot you reach is where the new leaf goes.

practice.title: Kth Smallest Element in a BST
practice.insight: An in-order walk visits the values from smallest to largest, so stop at the k-th node you visit.

practice.title: Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Search Tree
practice.insight: If both values are smaller than the node, go left, and if both are bigger, go right. Where they split is the answer.

practice.title: Convert Sorted Array to Binary Search Tree
practice.insight: Pick the middle value as the root, and build each half of the array into a subtree the same way.

practice.title: Binary Search Tree Iterator
practice.insight: It is an in-order walk you can pause. A stack that holds the path of left children is all the state you need.

practice.title: Minimum Absolute Difference in BST
practice.insight: The closest pair of values are neighbours in sorted order, and an in-order walk hands you sorted order for free.

practice.title: Trim a Binary Search Tree
practice.insight: If a node is below the range, its whole left subtree is too, so the answer can only come from its right side. Mirror that for a node above the range.

practice.title: Balance a Binary Search Tree
practice.insight: Read the values out in order, then rebuild the tree from the middle of that sorted list, as when converting a sorted array.
